question: The Spanish Government recently announced its intention both to not allow the automatic extension of concessions for the occupation of Spain’s maritime-terrestrial public domain, and to grant all the concessions by public tender. Those and other changes seek to bring Spanish legislation into line with the Services Directive.

Spain’s implementation of that directive has led, for example, to an infringement procedure being opened against the Spanish Coastal Law adopted in 2013 for its failure to ensure that the selection procedure for granting coastal-area concessions was transparent and impartial, as well as for its inclusion of the option to extend existing concessions for up to seventy-five years without justification.
Does the Commission consider the automatic extension of existing concessions for up to seventy-five years, as permitted by the 2013 law, to be lawful under the Services Directive?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.4.

2026) As indicated in the reply to parliamentary question E-003057/20241, the Commission issued a reasoned opinion in this case INFR(2022)41212 given that the Spanish legislation, as adopted in 1988, 2013 and 2014, does not provide for the obligation to use an impartial and transparent selection procedure to award concessions to build permanent premises on the coastal public domain and carry out economic activities therein.

Moreover, it does allow for the extension of certain concessions for up to 75 years. The Commission took the view that this legislation breaches both the obligations under the Services Directive3 and the principle of the freedom of establishment enshrined in Article 49 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.
The Commission remains in close contact with the competent Spanish authorities to pursue the constructive dialogue in relation to this case.
